name: AI Devices in Europe: MDR, IVDR and the AI Act
blurb: The two regimes an AI device must satisfy in the EU.
title: AI Devices in Europe: MDR, IVDR and the AI Act
answer: In Europe an AI medical device must meet the Medical Device or In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation and, where it needs notified body review, the AI Act's requirements for high risk systems: data quality, robustness, transparency, human oversight and cybersecurity. Guidance has started to align the two so a single conformity assessment can cover both.

reading.body:
An AI medical device sold in Europe must satisfy the Medical Device Regulation or the In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation, and the AI Act as well where notified body review is required.

The two regimes overlap rather than stack. The AI Act's high risk obligations cover data quality, robustness, transparency, human oversight and cybersecurity, and those are the same properties a notified body already examines under MDR or IVDR. Guidance has begun to align the two so one conformity assessment can serve both.

For a medtech team the practical consequence is that the AI Act work belongs inside the existing quality system, not beside it. A parallel compliance track duplicates evidence that the device regulator is already collecting. The AI Act entered into force on 1 August 2024 and treats AI medical devices needing notified body assessment as high risk.

What this does not cover is timing. The data gives no dates for when the high risk obligations begin to apply to devices, no detail on how the aligned assessment is conducted, and no view of devices that fall outside notified body review. It also says nothing about compute, hosting or the physical infrastructure a device runs on, so no conclusion about those can be drawn from it.

terms.line: The field of computer science dedicated to creating systems that perform tasks typically requiring human intelligence: understanding language, recognizing patterns, making decisions.

The formal process of demonstrating a product meets regulatory requirements before it goes to market. Depending on classification it is self-assessed or third-party assessed, and the difference determines cost, timeline, and who signs.
The 2026 package of targeted amendments to the EU AI Act, deferring high-risk deadlines and restructuring conformity assessment.

The requirement that a person can understand, intervene in, and override AI decisions. Mandated for high-risk uses under the EU AI Act, and only real when the human has the time, information, and authority to actually intervene.
An accredited organization designated to carry out third-party conformity assessment under EU product law.

510(k), De Novo and PMA for AI Devices

explainer:
In the European Union a medical device needs a CE mark under the Medical Device Regulation or, for diagnostics, the In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation. Most software devices fall into classes that require assessment by a notified body, an independent organisation designated to check conformity. The AI Act adds a second layer: AI that is a safety component of such a device, or is itself such a device, is classed as high risk.

High risk systems must meet AI Act requirements on risk management, data governance, technical documentation, record keeping, transparency, human oversight, accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity. Much of this overlaps with what MDR already requires, and the intent is a single conformity assessment by the notified body covering both. Makers should extend their existing quality and risk processes to cover the AI specific requirements, especially data governance and bias, rather than building separate systems.

developments.text: The AI Act entered into force, treating AI medical devices that require notified body assessment as high risk.
